You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION ONE: LOGIC**

**1)** *Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow:*

> One day, some young boys decided to contribute money to buy a dog for their barbecue, but the bully among them refused to contribute. As the barbecue was getting ready, the dreaded bully came to the scene and told the boys that either they give his share or he will take everything. One of the boys said to the bully: "if you want to partake in the barbecue, you have to pay your contribution; and if you have no money, you leave us alone." The youngest among them had foreseen the threat and prepared himself to face the bully, should he come to disturb them.
>
> When the bully attempted to seize the barbecue, the youngest one sprayed a peppery solution into his eyes rendering him powerless. When he was asked why he did that, he said he had learned it from some elders. When the news went round, one girl said that all bullies are criminals.

**Questions**
incertitudes: Question 1(a)(i) : « the converse of the contrapositive of "All bullies are truants" » est lu comme : contrapositive = « All non-truants are non-bullies » (A), converse = « All non-bullies are non-truants » (permutation des termes). Dans le système booléen, la conversion simple n'est valide que pour E et I : cette converse n'est donc pas validement inférée, ce que le corrigé dit expressément. La converse par limitation (« Some non-bullies are non-truants ») n'existe que dans le système aristotélicien. La clé du jury est inconnue : l'énoncé (« stating the rule that validates conversion ») et la sous-question (ii) (qui suppose une proposition universelle ayant un subalterne) ont guidé cette lecture (vérifié par énumération de modèles : la converse de A est invalide dans les deux systèmes ; le subalterne est invalide dans le seul système booléen).

Question 1(c)(i)-(iii) : la disjonction de la menace du bully (« either they give his share or he will take everything ») est choisie comme proposition disjonctive du texte ; son Modus Ponendo Tollens est invalide car la disjonction est inclusive (contre-ligne de la table de vérité : les deux membres vrais). Si le jury lisait la disjonction comme exclusive, le MPT serait valide : le corrigé le précise.

Question 1(b)(iii) : l'issue « entre les cornes » proposée (le bully ne veut pas participer aux conditions communes et n'est pas sans argent) est un exemple raisonnable ; d'autres réponses seraient acceptables. Les deux autres manières de répondre à un dilemme sont mentionnées sans être développées.

Question 1(e)(i) : la fausse généralisation (« all bullies are criminals », hasty generalisation) est retenue ; le corrigé mentionne aussi l'appel à la force (ad baculum) et le faux dilemme dans la menace du bully, également acceptables.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Identify:

(i) Give the converse of the contrapositive of "All bullies are truants", in the Boolean system stating the rule that validates conversion. (3 marks)

(ii) Explain why the subaltern of a(i) would be illicit in the Boolean system. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $B$ = bullies and $T$ = truants. "All bullies are truants" is an **A** proposition: *All $B$ are $T$*.

**(i) The converse of the contrapositive.**

- **Contrapositive** (obversion, conversion, obversion; valid for A and for O in both the Boolean and the Aristotelian systems): *All non-truants are non-bullies* (All non-$T$ are non-$B$).
- **Converse** of this contrapositive (subject and predicate exchanged, quality and quantity unchanged): **All non-bullies are non-truants** (All non-$B$ are non-$T$).

**The rule of conversion.** In the Boolean system conversion is validated only by **simple conversion** (exchange the subject and the predicate, keep the quality and the quantity), and this rule holds only for **E** and **I** propositions. An **A** proposition cannot be converted simply: "All non-bullies are non-truants" does **not** follow from "All non-truants are non-bullies" (counter-model: some non-bullies who are truants; drawing the converse would be the fallacy of *illicit conversion*). The only converse an A proposition has is the one **by limitation** (*per accidens*), "Some non-bullies are non-truants", and it depends on existential import, so it belongs to the Aristotelian system and not to the Boolean one.

**Answer (i):** the converse of the contrapositive is *All non-bullies are non-truants*; simple conversion (E and I only) is the rule that validates conversion in the Boolean system, so for this A proposition the converse is a formal transformation that is not validly inferred.

**(ii) Why the subaltern is illicit in the Boolean system.**

The subaltern of the universal a(i) is the particular of the same quality: **Some non-bullies are non-truants** (an **I** proposition).

- In the **Aristotelian** system the universal propositions have **existential import**: the subject class is assumed to have members, so $A \to I$ (subalternation) is allowed.
- In the **Boolean** system a universal proposition says only "if anything is a non-bully, it is a non-truant"; it does **not** assert that non-bullies exist, whereas a particular proposition does assert existence. "All non-bullies are non-truants" may therefore be true when there are **no** non-bullies at all (for instance if everybody is a bully), and then "Some non-bullies are non-truants" is false.
- So the move from the A to the I commits the **existential fallacy** (illicit subalternation): the conclusion asserts existence that the premise does not guarantee. Subalternation is not valid in the Boolean system.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Pick out:

(i) A conjunctive proposition suitable for a complex dilemma. (1 mark)

(ii) Use b(i) to build a complex affirmative dilemma. (3 marks)

(iii) Refute the dilemma in b(ii) by escaping between the horns. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $W$ = you want to partake in the barbecue; $C$ = you pay your contribution; $N$ = you have no money; $L$ = you leave us alone.

**(i) The conjunctive proposition.** The boy's words:

> *If you want to partake in the barbecue, you have to pay your contribution; and if you have no money, you leave us alone.*

It is a conjunction of **two conditionals** with **different antecedents and different consequents**: $(W \supset C)\cdot(N \supset L)$. This is exactly the major premise of a **complex** dilemma (in a simple dilemma the two conditionals would share a single antecedent or a single consequent).

**(ii) A complex affirmative (constructive) dilemma.** The minor premise *affirms the antecedents* in a disjunction; the conclusion is the disjunction of the consequents.

> If you want to partake in the barbecue, you have to pay your contribution; and if you have no money, you leave us alone.
> Either you want to partake in the barbecue or you have no money.
> Therefore, either you pay your contribution or you leave us alone.

Form: $(W \supset C)\cdot(N \supset L),\ W \vee N\ \therefore\ C \vee L$. It is valid (a truth table over the 16 combinations of $W, C, N, L$ has no row with true premises and a false conclusion).

**(iii) Escaping between the horns.** The two "horns" are the two alternatives of the minor premise, $W$ and $N$. To escape *between* them we show that the disjunction "either you want to partake or you have no money" is **false**, that is, that both alternatives are false together:

- the bully does **not** want to partake in the barbecue *on the common terms* (he wants to seize everything), **and**
- he does **not** lack money: he has the means to pay and simply refuses.

Then $W \vee N$ is false, the minor premise fails, and the dilemma does not force the conclusion "either you pay your contribution or you leave us alone". (The other two ways of meeting a dilemma are different: *grasping the dilemma by the horns* denies one of the conditionals, for instance "wanting to partake does not oblige one to pay"; the *rebuttal* constructs a counter-dilemma.)

*Condition:* escaping between the horns is possible only when the disjunction is **not exhaustive**, i.e. when a third alternative exists that makes both disjuncts false.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Identify:

(i) A disjunctive proposition from the passage. (1 mark)

(ii) Use c(i) to construct a *Modus Ponendo Tollens* argument. (2 marks)

(iii) Explain why the *Modus Ponendo Tollens* in c(ii) above is invalid. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $S$ = they give the bully his share; $E$ = he will take everything.

**(i) The disjunctive proposition.** The bully "told the boys that **either they give his share or he will take everything**": $S \vee E$.

**(ii) A Modus Ponendo Tollens (MPT).** MPT *affirms* one disjunct in the minor premise and *denies* the other in the conclusion.

> Either they give the bully his share or he will take everything.
> They give the bully his share.
> Therefore, he will not take everything.

Form: $S \vee E,\ S\ \therefore\ \sim E$.

**(iii) Why it is invalid.** MPT is valid only when the disjunction is **exclusive** (strong: "one or the other, but not both"). The bully's "either ... or" is **inclusive** (weak): both alternatives can be true together, since he can receive his share and still take everything (he is a bully). Affirming one disjunct therefore tells us nothing about the other. The truth table shows the counter-row:

| $S$ | $E$ | $S \vee E$ | $S$ | $\sim E$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | **T** | **T** | **F** |
| T | F | T | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | F |
| F | F | F | F | T |

In the first row both premises are true and the conclusion is false, so the argument is **invalid** (it commits the fallacy of affirming a disjunct). It would be valid only if the disjunction were read as exclusive.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Given the syllogism:

*All boys are thieves*
*All cheats are boys*
*Therefore some cheats are thieves*

(i) Explain why the syllogism above is invalid in the Boolean system. (2 marks)

(ii) Explain why it is valid in the Aristotelian system. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $T$ = thieves (major term $P$), $B$ = boys (middle term $M$), $C$ = cheats (minor term $S$).

| | Statement | Form |
|:-|:-|:-:|
| Major premise (A) | All boys are thieves | All $M$ are $P$ |
| Minor premise (A) | All cheats are boys | All $S$ are $M$ |
| Conclusion (I) | Therefore some cheats are thieves | Some $S$ are $P$ |

The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: **figure 1**; the mood is A-A-I. It is the form **AAI-1** (*Barbari*): the weakened form of Barbara (AAA-1).

**(i) Invalid in the Boolean system.** Both premises are **universal** and the conclusion is **particular**. In the Boolean system a universal proposition has no existential import: "All cheats are boys" is true even if there are no cheats at all. Take a universe with no cheats: both premises are true (vacuously), but "Some cheats are thieves" is false because it asserts that there are cheats. The syllogism commits the **existential fallacy** (a particular conclusion drawn from two universal premises) and is therefore invalid. (The valid conclusion in the Boolean system is only the universal one, "All cheats are thieves", by Barbara.)

**(ii) Valid in the Aristotelian system.** The Aristotelian system assumes **existential import**: every term (here "cheats", "boys", "thieves") denotes a non-empty class. Then:

1. From the premises, Barbara gives "All cheats are thieves" (the middle term "boys" is distributed in the major premise; the premises are affirmative and the conclusion is affirmative; no term is distributed in the conclusion without being distributed in a premise).
2. Since cheats exist, the **subalternation** of the A proposition gives the I proposition: "Some cheats are thieves".

So no counter-model exists once the classes are assumed non-empty (checked exhaustively with Python): the syllogism is valid in the Aristotelian system.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) Pick out:

(i) A fallacy from the passage above. (1 mark)

(ii) Explain how the fallacy in e(i) has been committed. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The fallacy:** **hasty generalisation** (sweeping generalisation from an unrepresentative case), committed by the girl who said "all bullies are criminals".

**(ii) How it is committed.**

- The girl's conclusion is a **universal** statement about **all** bullies. Her only evidence is the **single** incident she has heard of: one bully who tried to seize the barbecue. One case, or a small number of cases, is neither a **large** nor a **representative** sample of the whole class of bullies.
- She **assumes that what is true of one member is true of every member**, and she ignores the many bullies who have never committed a crime and the difference between bad behaviour and a criminal offence (the bully only attempted to take the food, and bullying is not necessarily a crime).
- Hence the premise (one bully acted wrongly) does not support the conclusion (all bullies are criminals): even if that bully were guilty, nothing would follow about bullies in general. The form is: $a$ is $F$ and $G$; therefore all $F$ are $G$.

(Another fallacy that can be picked out is the **appeal to force** (*argumentum ad baculum*) in the bully's threat "either they give his share or he will take everything": he tries to win by threatening harm instead of giving a reason. It also relies on a possible **false dilemma**.)
